schools.summary: Gill explains why the heir was chosen as confidant and places the house at Gibeah.
Henry reads the order as malice unashamed of itself and the friendship as providence against it.
Clarke measures the danger by the standing orders given to every officer and soldier.
Ellicott prefers a stricter rendering of Saul's words and traces the murderous impulse through three stages.

debates.question: What does the openness of the order against David show?

sides.position: Malice that could give no reason and was not ashamed to avow it
A danger so complete that only God's particular interposition could meet it
An impulse grown from paroxysm to plot to open speech

outliers.note: Alone in preferring the rendering that Saul spoke of intending David's death, with the Greek and Syriac behind it.

1.pericope_label: Saul spake to Jonathan to kill David; Jonathan delighted much in David

schools.summary: Gill itemises the plea and reads the king as genuinely wrought upon for the time.
Henry's sentence on God inclining Saul's heart is carried into this span inside Wesley's note.
Clarke calls the pleading short and unanswerable, and Wesley weighs what it cost the pleader.
Keil and Delitzsch set out the clauses of the argument, and Ellicott turns it into direct speech about the day of the giant.

sides.position: Meant at the time, with a real change felt for the present
A heart touched for a short while by something of the old noble spirit
Sincere enough to reverse the previous day's orders

outliers.note: The only voice in this chapter quoting another commentator by name, attributing to Henry the sentence that God inclined Saul's heart.

themes: he put his life in his hand
in his presence as in times past
4.pericope_label: Let not the king sin against his servant; Jonathan brought David to Saul

schools.summary: Gill takes the fighting for skirmishes and the relapse for a returning disorder.
Henry praises a man who went on serving with sword and harp, and makes indulged passion the invitation to the evil spirit.
Clarke credits bodily agility for the escape, and Wesley has the devil watching his opportunity.
Keil and Delitzsch name a higher cause for the madness, and Ellicott argues at length about what an evil spirit of the Lord can mean.

debates.question: How is the evil spirit from the Lord to be understood?

sides.position: A madness inflicted by Jehovah, marking the hardness of heart he was given up to
Indulged passion inviting the devil, the disorder beginning in a man's own sins and follies
A fallen spirit permitted, for reasons hidden from us, to plague a soul that had deserted God

outliers.note: Alone in quoting Browning's poem on Saul, and in setting out a doctrine of evil spirits to explain the phrase.

8.pericope_label: Saul sought to smite David with the javelin; he slipped away

schools.summary: Gill locates the house and supplies two scriptural parallels for the letting down.
Henry makes the wife given as a snare into the protector, and reads the psalm written that night as a composed mind in a hurry.
Clarke works out where the watchers stood and why the back of the house defeated them.
Keil and Delitzsch report the escape as the narrative gives it, and Ellicott dates the long wanderings from this flight.

debates.question: Why the window rather than a door?

sides.position: Every door was watched, and clearing the house by the sword was not lawful
The back of the house had neither door nor way through, so the ambush was eluded without being passed

outliers.note: Alone in supplying the parallels of the spies let down at Jericho and the apostle let down at Damascus.

11.pericope_label: Michal let David down through a window; he fled and escaped

schools.summary: Gill stacks up the rabbinic accounts of the teraphim and answers one of them himself.
Clarke keeps to what the scene requires of the image, and Wesley to the glimmering light of a sick man's room.
Ellicott gives the word's grammar and history, and Keil and Delitzsch weigh the wife's answer as a prevarication she thought justifiable.

debates.question: Was the fifty-ninth psalm written on this night?

sides.position: Yes, as the title given to it says
Probably David's, and probably with this danger in mind, but the title is not confirmed by the psalm's own references

outliers.note: Alone in canvassing the Jewish explanations of the teraphim, from figures cast under a constellation to a kind of dial.

themes: bring him up in the bed
13.pericope_label: Michal took an image and laid it in the bed; Saul sent to take him

schools.summary: Gill traces how the news reached Saul, through officious persons who had watched where the two men went.
Henry gives three reasons for the flight to Samuel and reads the escalation as providence unrecognised.
Clarke has the prophet keep him at his school, and Wesley adds safety to comfort and direction.
Ellicott explains Naioth as a cluster of dwellings, and Keil and Delitzsch defend the singular verb and the rare word for the company.

debates.question: Why did David flee to Samuel rather than to kinsmen or a friendly city?

sides.position: To have a failing faith renewed, to get a prophet's advice, and for the company of those who praise God
For advice, and because the prophet judged it best to keep him there
Because the old seer's house was a sanctuary no pursuit would enter

outliers.note: Alone in defending the singular verb for what the messengers saw against the charge of a copyist's error.

18.pericope_label: David fled to Samuel to Ramah; they dwelt at Naioth

schools.summary: Gill marks the effrontery of sending officers into a sacred place, and what the news back to Saul actually was.
Clarke has the officers partake of the same influence, and Wesley compares the inspiration to Balaam's.
Ellicott calls the event outside ordinary experience and borrows Ewald's reconstruction of it; Keil and Delitzsch record the second and third companies.

sides.position: The Spirit of God coming upon the messengers, which is outside ordinary experience
An inspiration like Balaam's, which carried their minds off the errand
The same influence and the same exercise as the company they found

outliers.note: Alone in explaining why a presiding prophet was needed: preparation beforehand, improvement afterwards, and the detecting of pretended raptures.

20.pericope_label: The Spirit of God was upon the messengers, and they also prophesied

schools.summary: Gill traces the route from Gibeah and limits the stripping to the upper garments.
Clarke dates the seizure from the well and Wesley renders the posture as a fall to the earth, God keeping the king in chains.
Keil and Delitzsch gloss the word for nakedness and the repeated phrase, and Ellicott asks what the outpouring on a faithless king meant.

debates.question: What did the Spirit's coming upon Saul mean?

sides.position: Madness, as the Chaldee is taken to say — or rather a last pleading with the anointed man, forgotten when the excitement passed
A providence that held him as in chains until David was out of reach
A divine influence on king and men alike, to keep them from touching David

outliers.note: Alone in noting that the repeated phrase shows the king fell into the same ecstatic state as his servants.

22.pericope_label: Is Saul also among the prophets?
